title: You Can Be Better Than Ofsted
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that schools are drowning in data they do not understand, treating all of it as equally meaningful when one year of data or a comparison to a national average tells a limited or misleading story. He offers school leaders a light-touch approach to external data (Progress 8 by subject and group, removing EAL students, the FFT comparator schools) and to internal data (finding teachers who consistently beat the trend over three years). A worked case study of a fictional school shows how a desk-top analysis can predict an Ofsted grade. The move is to make data a tool for learning from the best subject or teacher rather than for ranking.
points: Small group sizes and single-year figures make much of school data statistically unreliable.
Comparing against FFT similar schools gives a fairer picture of context than national averages.
Looking for teachers with high three-year progress reveals a teacher effect worth learning from.
The case study shows a standout department (Humanities) as the model other departments should study.
A simple desk-top analysis can usually predict an Ofsted grade, apart from schools with behaviour or safeguarding problems.
quotes: We obsess over data. We have new catch phrases, where we “drill down” without ever worrying about the “confidence interval”.
Data tells a story. One year of data, tells a limited story. The comparison of your school to a national average, tells a misleading story.

Use the FFT comparator schools website to see how your school performed against the 51 most similar schools in the country. This will tell you how well you are doing compared to schools with similar contexts.
Use your internal data to find individual teachers who appear to be bucking the trend - doing better than the rest of their team. Compare teachers teaching similar groups.
Recalculate your Progress 8 by taking out EAL students. They achieve about +0.5 nationally.
Although 2022 results need to be treated with caution because of the uneven impact of the pandemic, a desk top analysis of data suggests that the best fit for the school is ‘good’.
